parts.passageHtml:
You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 1-13, which are based on Reading Passage 1 below.

Health in the Wild

Many animals seem able to treat their illnesses themselves. Humans may have a thing or two to learn from them.

For the past decade, Dr Cindy Engel, a lecturer in Environmental Sciences at Britain's Open University, has been collating examples of self-medicating behaviour in wild animals. In a talk on the subject, she explained that the idea that animals can treat themselves had generally been regarded with some scepticism by other animal behaviourists. However, a growing number of researchers came to believe that wild animals can and do deal with their own medical needs.

Dr William Karesh of the Wildlife Conservation Society in New York, for example, studied the health of a wide range of wild animals, including anaconda snakes, macaws, penguins, impala and buffalo. The animals were mostly in good physical condition, which is not surprising since weak individuals quickly die in the wild. However, blood tests showed that many had encountered unpleasant viral and bacterial diseases in the past, including diseases that are often fatal in captive animals even when treated by vets. Moreover, when healthy wild animals are brought into captivity, their health often deteriorates unless great care is taken over their living conditions. Such observations suggest that wild animals can do something to keep themselves healthy that captive animals cannot.

One example of self-medication was discovered in 1987. Dr Michael Huffman and Mohamedi Seifu, working in the Mahale Mountains National Park in Tanzania, noticed that local chimpanzees suffering from intestinal worms would dose themselves with the pith—the white substance between the skin and the flesh—of a plant called Vernonia. This plant produces poisonous chemicals called terpenes. Its pith contains a concentration strong enough to kill gut parasites but not strong enough to kill chimpanzees—or humans, for that matter. Local people use the pith for the same purpose.

Since the Vernonia-eating chimpanzees were discovered, further evidence has suggested that animals often consume substances for medical rather than nutritional reasons. Many species, for example, eat soil, a behaviour known as geophagy. An earlier explanation was that soil supplied minerals such as salt. However, geophagy also occurs in areas where the soil is not a useful source of minerals, and in places where minerals can be obtained more easily from plants known to be rich in them. This suggests that animals gain some other benefit from eating soil.

Researchers therefore proposed that soil—and particularly the clay it contains—may help to detoxify the defensive poisons produced by some plants to prevent themselves from being eaten. Evidence for the detoxifying effect of clay came in 1999 from an experiment carried out on macaws by Dr James Gilardi and his colleagues at the University of California, Davis. Macaws eat seeds containing alkaloids, a group of chemicals that includes some highly toxic substances, such as strychnine. In the wild, the birds are frequently seen perched on eroding riverbanks eating clay. Dr Gilardi fed one group of macaws a mixture of harmless alkaloid and clay, and a second group only the alkaloid. Several hours later, the birds that had eaten the clay had 60% less alkaloid in their bloodstreams than those that had not, supporting the hypothesis that clay has a detoxifying effect.

A third example of animal self-medication involves the use of mechanical scouring to remove gut parasites. In 1972, Dr Richard Wrangham, a researcher at the Gombe Stream Reserve in Tanzania, noticed chimpanzees eating the leaves of a tree called Aspilia. The chimpanzees selected the leaves carefully by testing them in their mouths. After choosing a leaf, a chimpanzee would fold it into a fan and swallow it. Some were seen wrinkling their noses as they swallowed the leaves, suggesting that the experience was unpleasant. Later, undigested leaves were found on the forest floor.

Dr Wrangham correctly guessed that the leaves served a medicinal purpose—one of the earliest interpretations of a behaviour pattern now known as self-medication. However, his explanation of the mechanism was wrong. He and other researchers assumed that Aspilia released a drug, which led to more than two decades of phytochemical research aimed at identifying the chemical the chimpanzees were seeking. By the 1990s, however, chimpanzees across Africa had been observed swallowing leaves from 19 different species that appeared to have few suitable chemicals in common. The drug hypothesis therefore became increasingly doubtful.

Dr Huffman eventually identified the mechanism by examining what passed through the chimpanzees rather than concentrating only on what they swallowed. He found that the expelled leaves were covered with intestinal worms. The feature common to all 19 species of leaves was a surface covered in microscopic hooks. These hooks caught the worms and dragged them from their position in the gut.

Dr Engel has also considered how knowledge of animal self-medication might be used to improve the health of livestock. Humans may have something to learn as well—and may already have done so. Geophagy, for example, is common in many parts of the world. Medical stalls in African markets frequently sell tablets made from different types of clay for different medical conditions.

Africans brought to the Americas as slaves continued this tradition, although their owners often treated the practice with contempt. Yet, as Dr Engel points out, Rwandan mountain gorillas eat a type of clay rather similar to kaolinite, the main ingredient of many over-the-counter medicines sold in the West for digestive complaints. Eating soil, therefore, can sometimes have genuine medical benefits.

parts.name: Passage 2
parts.passageHtml:
You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14-26, which are based on Reading Passage 2.

Babies Cry in Their Mother Tongue

A newborn baby's cry may sound much the same to sleep-deprived parents around the world, but scientists say that comparisons of babies only a few days old reveal similarities between their cries and the language spoken by their parents. The likely explanation lies in the different intonation patterns of their mother tongues, which babies begin to perceive before birth and later reproduce.

A

It is already known that human foetuses become attentive listeners during the final trimester of pregnancy. “The mother's voice in particular is sensed early on,” explains Professor Amelia Finlayson of the Institute for Human Cognitive and Brain Sciences in Leipzig. “Human foetuses perceive information filtered at around 400 hertz, but they cannot hear the actual words. It is a bit like holding your head under water while someone is talking beside the bath.”

B

Finlayson's research suggests that newborn babies probably cannot distinguish between accents such as Welsh and Northern Scottish, or between Low German and Upper Bavarian. They can, however, recognise major differences in the intonation patterns of their respective mother tongues. The Leipzig researchers had demonstrated this in an earlier experiment using physiological measurements from babies aged three to four months. The babies wore hoods fitted with electrodes while recordings of different intonation patterns were played to them. Their brainwaves responded to the differences even when they were asleep.

C

Dr Katya Williams of the University of Würzburg was among the first to suggest, in her PhD thesis, that babies' crying might represent a stage in linguistic development. “It used to be thought that a baby's cry was simply an alarm signal to call its mother,” Williams explains. “This assumption was challenged when we noticed that cries are not the same from week to week. What biological purpose would that serve? If a fire siren sounded different every day, we might eventually fail to recognise it.”

D

This raised the question of whether babies' cries already displayed the intonation patterns of their different mother tongues. To investigate this, the Leipzig brain researchers and the University of Würzburg team collaborated with colleagues at the Laboratory of Cognitive Sciences and Linguistics at the École Normale Supérieure in Paris. German and French babies were selected because the intonation patterns of these two languages differ particularly clearly. For example, the German word Papa is stressed on the first syllable, whereas in French the stress falls on the second.

E

The three research groups compared recordings from 60 healthy newborns between two and five days old: 30 from French-speaking families and 30 from German-speaking families. Whenever the babies were hungry, thirsty or simply wanted their mothers and began to cry, the researchers recorded them. More than 20 hours of recordings were subsequently entered into a computer for analysis.

F

The striking result, published in the journal Current Biology, was that only a few days after birth, babies were already using acoustic information perceived in the uterus to adapt their vocal production to their mother tongue. The cries of the German babies generally began loudly and at a high pitch before following a downward curve, whereas the French babies more often produced a rising melodic contour. In other words, the babies reproduced characteristic intonation patterns of the languages to which they had been exposed. The researchers argued that these cries represented attempts to communicate specifically with their mothers. “Newborns are probably highly motivated to imitate their mother's behaviour in order to attract her and foster bonding and therefore physical nourishment,” they wrote.

G

The findings also support the hypothesis that linguistic development does not begin only at around nine or ten months, when babies start producing language-like babbling such as “mam-mam-mam” or “ba-ba-ba”, but with the very first sounds they produce. “We are born to learn language. And that starts right away,” says Williams. Williams's colleague, Walter Meade, found that this early sensitivity to the melodic features of language helps infants subsequently learn their mother tongue. “The melodic patterns practised in crying are building blocks for later sound production, from gurgling and babbling through to the first words and sentences,” he explains.

H

The results also highlighted a difference between human infants and other primates. According to Williams, the “crying melody” of baby chimpanzees is closely associated with the build-up and release of pressure in the lungs rather than being generated by a mental process. “In comparison with the sounds of other primates, the cries of a newborn human baby display a remarkable repertoire of melodic and rhythmic variations,” she adds. “Our babies are expert vocalists compared with other animals. Perhaps that offers some small consolation to exhausted parents.”

You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14-26, which are based on Reading Passage 2.

Babies Cry in Their Mother Tongue

A newborn baby's cry may sound much the same to sleep-deprived parents around the world, but scientists say that comparisons of babies only a few days old reveal similarities between their cries and the language spoken by their parents. The likely explanation lies in the different intonation patterns of their mother tongues, which babies begin to perceive before birth and later reproduce.

A

It is already known that human foetuses become attentive listeners during the final trimester of pregnancy. “The mother's voice in particular is sensed early on,” explains Professor Amelia Finlayson of the Institute for Human Cognitive and Brain Sciences in Leipzig. “Human foetuses perceive information filtered at around 400 hertz, but they cannot hear the actual words. It is a bit like holding your head under water while someone is talking beside the bath.”

B

Finlayson's research suggests that newborn babies probably cannot distinguish between accents such as Welsh and Northern Scottish, or between Low German and Upper Bavarian. They can, however, recognise major differences in the intonation patterns of their respective mother tongues. The Leipzig researchers had demonstrated this in an earlier experiment using physiological measurements from babies aged three to four months. The babies wore hoods fitted with electrodes while recordings of different intonation patterns were played to them. Their brainwaves responded to the differences even when they were asleep.

C

Dr Katya Williams of the University of Würzburg was among the first to suggest, in her PhD thesis, that babies' crying might represent a stage in linguistic development. “It used to be thought that a baby's cry was simply an alarm signal to call its mother,” Williams explains. “This assumption was challenged when we noticed that cries are not the same from week to week. What biological purpose would that serve? If a fire siren sounded different every day, we might eventually fail to recognise it.”

D

This raised the question of whether babies' cries already displayed the intonation patterns of their different mother tongues. To investigate this, the Leipzig brain researchers and the University of Würzburg team collaborated with colleagues at the Laboratory of Cognitive Sciences and Linguistics at the École Normale Supérieure in Paris. German and French babies were selected because the intonation patterns of these two languages differ particularly clearly. For example, the German word Papa is stressed on the first syllable, whereas in French the stress falls on the second.

E

The three research groups compared recordings from 60 healthy newborns between two and five days old: 30 from French-speaking families and 30 from German-speaking families. Whenever the babies were hungry, thirsty or simply wanted their mothers and began to cry, the researchers recorded them. More than 20 hours of recordings were subsequently entered into a computer for analysis.

F

The striking result, published in the journal Current Biology, was that only a few days after birth, babies were already using acoustic information perceived in the uterus to adapt their vocal production to their mother tongue. The cries of the German babies generally began loudly and at a high pitch before following a downward curve, whereas the French babies more often produced a rising melodic contour. In other words, the babies reproduced characteristic intonation patterns of the languages to which they had been exposed. The researchers argued that these cries represented attempts to communicate specifically with their mothers. “Newborns are probably highly motivated to imitate their mother's behaviour in order to attract her and foster bonding and therefore physical nourishment,” they wrote.

G

The findings also support the hypothesis that linguistic development does not begin only at around nine or ten months, when babies start producing language-like babbling such as “mam-mam-mam” or “ba-ba-ba”, but with the very first sounds they produce. “We are born to learn language. And that starts right away,” says Williams. Williams's colleague, Walter Meade, found that this early sensitivity to the melodic features of language helps infants subsequently learn their mother tongue. “The melodic patterns practised in crying are building blocks for later sound production, from gurgling and babbling through to the first words and sentences,” he explains.

H

The results also highlighted a difference between human infants and other primates. According to Williams, the “crying melody” of baby chimpanzees is closely associated with the build-up and release of pressure in the lungs rather than being generated by a mental process. “In comparison with the sounds of other primates, the cries of a newborn human baby display a remarkable repertoire of melodic and rhythmic variations,” she adds. “Our babies are expert vocalists compared with other animals. Perhaps that offers some small consolation to exhausted parents.”

parts.passageHtml:
You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 27-40, which are based on Reading Passage 3.

THEORIES OF PLANET FORMATION QUESTIONED

A

The traditional view in astronomy has been that planets form slowly as material comes together within the disk of gas, dust and ice surrounding a young star. First, gravity gathers particles of dust that merge to form boulder-sized bodies, which in turn combine into progressively larger objects. In about a million years, these develop into rocky planets such as Earth and Mars. Over the next few million years, gas from the disk settles around some of these solid bodies, causing them to grow much larger and eventually become giants such as Saturn and Jupiter. This theory of planet formation is known as the core-accretion model. However, several astronomers have argued that this model may not provide a complete explanation of how planets form.

B

These astronomers have developed an alternative theory in which planets as massive as Jupiter, whether orbiting our Sun or a distant star, can form within only a few hundred years rather than over millions of years. Both theories begin with the same reservoir of planet-forming material. A spinning cloud of gas, dust and ice rapidly flattens into a structure known as a proto-planetary disk, and gravity then causes material within the disk to gather into planet-sized objects. The main difference between the two models lies in the speed at which this clustering occurs and the size of the initial clumps.

C

According to the core-accretion model, the formation of Jupiter required a solid core with five to ten times the mass of Earth to develop first. This process would have taken about a million years. Most astronomers believe that the large core then had sufficient gravity to attract a huge amount of gas from the surrounding proto-planetary disk, creating a planet of Jupiter's enormous size. Under the core-accretion model, such gas giants may take as long as ten million years to form.

D

Lucio Mayer of Zurich University argues that this process takes several million years too long. Direct telescope observations suggest that proto-planetary disks do not survive for more than about seven million years, while studies of the environments in which stars form indicate that many disks may disappear much sooner. Mayer points out that most stars in the Milky Way form within dense clouds of gas, dust and ice. The stars can be extremely hot, and the ultraviolet light they emit can evaporate a proto-planetary disk in less than 100,000 years. Under the core-accretion model, this would not leave enough time for a Jupiter-like planet to form.

E

Computer simulations have also shown that when individual stars form, the gravitational pull between them can destroy the outer gaseous parts of proto-planetary disks in 100,000 years or less. Thomas Quinn of the University of Washington therefore concludes that if a gas giant cannot form quickly, it will probably never form. He also argues that if the core-accretion model is correct, gas giants such as Jupiter should be rare. Yet by the time of these studies, astronomers had identified more than one hundred planets as large as Jupiter outside our solar system.

F

Quinn and his colleagues analysed the standard core-accretion model to investigate whether giant planets could form more quickly. They examined the work of Gerard Kuiper, who in the 1950s had proposed that rapid formation was possible. Alan P. Boss of the Carnegie Institute carried out more extensive work on the subject in the late 1980s. Using computer simulations, he was surprised to find that gravity could cause a proto-planetary disk, after only a few orbits of its parent star, to break into clumps as large as an average planet. These clumps would continue to attract gas, ice and dust. This alternative process is known as the gravitational-instability model of planet formation.

G

Calculations have suggested a further problem for the traditional theory: many of the solid bodies that might eventually become the rocky cores of Jupiter-sized planets could spiral into their parent stars before the giant planets had time to form. Further analysis has also identified other processes that could make a proto-planetary disk unstable and cause it to split into large fragments. For example, electrically charged material could accumulate within a disk and lead to fragmentation. Alternatively, a powerful gravitational disturbance, such as the pull of a nearby passing star, could destabilise the disk.

H

Nevertheless, the gravitational-instability model has difficulties of its own. It is mathematically complicated and requires sophisticated computer simulations. As a result, researchers have not yet studied such simulations for long enough to establish conclusively that the model can produce massive planets.

I

In response, Mayer argues that his team has carried out an unusually extensive simulation based on the gravitational-instability model. They spent two years refining calculations to track the development of a proto-planetary disk over a period of one thousand years, longer than previous simulations had done. Mayer and his colleagues also had relevant experience from earlier simulations of the formation and evolution of galaxies. Through this work, they had already developed fast computer code capable of running in parallel on machines with hundreds of processors, and this expertise helped them investigate the gravitational-instability model.
